entries.title: Luke 1:1
segments: Forasmuch as many have taken in hand, etc.  A proof that many attempts to give an account of what our Lord did and said had already been made.  Though, from Luke's point of view, these early narratives were inadequate and incomplete, his language suggests that they were substantially accurate as sources of information.  Among them, most probably, were fragmentary accounts that were highly important and useful, such as collections of our Lord's sayings, especially the parables and discourses.  Many Biblical scholars think that the Gospel according to Mark was written before Luke began his narrative and that it was one of Luke's sources.  The fact that no mention is made of Mark does not indicate the contrary, as the custom of the time permitted it.

entries.title: Luke 1:2
segments: Even as they delivered them unto us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses. The reader is liable to misapprehend this passage on account of the position of 'who,' which immediately follows 'us.'  It is not meant that Luke and his friends or companions were eyewitnesses of the doings of our Lord.  The eyewitnesses and ministers were chiefly the apostles and disciples.

entries.title: Luke 1:3
segments:
To write unto thee in order. That is, to give a connected historical account in which what precedes prepares for and explains what follows.
 

 
Most excellent Theophilus. Theophilus (beloved of God) was probably a prominent Roman citizen who had become a Christian convert.  'Most excellent' was the form of address due to one of his knightly rank.  The same title was given to Felix and Festus (

entries.title: Luke 1:5
segments:
Of the course of Abijah. A 'course' was a selected number or group of priests to whom was assigned in rotation the conduct of the Temple services for a week.  There were twenty-four courses, of which Abijah's was the eighth.
 

 
Elizabeth. Or, Elisheba (one whose oath is by God).

entries.title: Luke 1:6
segments: Righteous before God. Not without sin, but righteous according to the requirements of the Mosaic Law.

entries.title: Luke 1:7
segments: They had no child. Childlessness was looked upon among the Jews not only as a misfortune, but also as a reproach.  The childless family could never hope to give the Messiah to the world.

entries.title: Luke 1:9
segments:
His lot. He was chosen by lot.
 

 
And burn incense. The incense altar, which was made of acacia wood thickly plated with gold, was before the veil of the Holy of Holies.  To burn incense upon the altar was the highest and most prized priestly function.  It signified that the prayers of the people had found favor with God.

entries.title: Luke 1:10
segments: The people were praying without. The Temple was less used for prayer than for the various sacrificial offerings.

entries.title: Luke 1:11
segments: The right side. Or, the south side.  The right side was traditionally associated with righteousness and with good tidings or other good fortune.  See

entries.title: Luke 1:13
segments: John. (Jehovah is gracious).

entries.title: Luke 1:15
segments: He shall drink no wine nor strong drink. John was a life member of the Nazirites, a Jewish order consecrated to the service of God.  They wore their hair long, abstained from strong drink and kept themselves free from ceremonial defilement under the Mosaic law.

entries.title: Luke 1:17
segments: He shall go before his face. That is, he shall be the forerunner of the Messiah.

entries.title: Luke 1:19
segments: Gabriel. (The mighty man of God).  One of the two angels named in the New Testament, the other being Michael (who is like God?).  See

.
 

 
That stand in the presence of God. Or, one of the angels of the presence.  See

entries.title: Luke 1:20
segments: Thou shalt be silent. This was the angel's answer to the question of Zacharias in
.  The priest, doubting, had asked for a sign, which was given him as a penalty in the form of his own dumbness.

entries.title: Luke 1:21
segments: Marvelled while he tarried. They wondered why his ministrations at the altar of incense lasted so long, and they feared that he had incurred the divine displeasure by some neglect or imperfect performance of his duties.

entries.title: Luke 1:22
segments: When he came out, he could not speak. Being dumb, he was unable to pronounce the priestly blessing for which the people were waiting.

entries.title: Luke 1:23
segments: The days of his ministration. The week chosen for the priests of Abijah's course.

entries.title: Luke 1:26
segments:
In the sixth month. After the conception of John the Baptist.
 

 
Named Nazareth. See note on
.  The word 'named' suggests that Luke wrote for readers who knew little about Palestine.

entries.title: Luke 1:27
segments:
Betrothed. The betrothal of a Jewish maiden was more binding and significant than a similar ceremony is with us.  It implied that the bridegroom had paid to the father of the prospective bride a sum of money, by which payment the control of the father over his daughter had passed to the bridegroom.  Betrothal ordinarily took place a year before marriage.
 

 
Mary. The same name as Miriam and Marah.

entries.title: Luke 1:31
segments: Shalt call his name Jesus. 'Jesus' was the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, Jeshua, or Jehosua (Jehovah is salvation).  See

entries.title: Luke 1:32
segments: He shall be great, etc.  Mary at this time could not have understood the sublime meanings of the angel's message, known to the world as the Annunciation; but she received the message in humble and obedient faith, being in this respect in marked contrast to the aged priest Zacharias (

entries.title: Luke 1:36
segments: Thy kinswoman. The degree of relationship is unknown.

entries.title: Luke 1:39
segments:
In these days. Probably within a few weeks after the angel had departed.
 

 
Into the hill country. The elevated parts of Judea, Samaria and lower Galilee.  In Canaan as divided among the twelve tribes the hill country included the mountainous districts of Ephraim, Benjamin and Judah.
 

 
With haste. As Mary was now betrothed to Joseph, her sudden departure from her home in Nazareth, where by Jewish custom she was bound to remain apart from her future husband until her marriage, could only result from her knowledge that the angel's prediction was true.
 

 
Into a city of Judah. 'Judah' here means Judea; but the name of the city is unknown.  Some scholars have conjectured that it was Juttah, one of the cities set apart for the priesthood.

entries.title: Luke 1:43
segments: The mother of my Lord. Elizabeth knew that the Son born to Mary would be the Messiah.

entries.title: Luke 1:46
segments: My soul doth magnify the Lord. These and the following words of

constitute the historic Christian hymn known as the Magnificat, an utterance of praise and thanksgiving by the Virgin Mary for the blessing and honor vouchsafed to her by God in the conception and birth of Jesus Christ.  It has been used in public church services since the sixth century.  Although a Christian hymn, its devotional feeling and spiritual outlook are Jewish.  Mary was far from fully comprehending the truth of which she was the vehicle.  Only the life and death of Jesus and the Christian experience of all succeeding ages could reveal the full meaning of her words.

entries.title: Luke 1:47
segments: God my Savior. That is, Jehovah, Savior not only from sin, but Deliverer from the Roman Empire or other foreign power. Much spiritual growth was needed before she knew her Son to be the Savior of the world.

entries.title: Luke 1:48
segments: All generations shall call me blessed. Spoken as a prophecy, which has been in part fulfilled.

entries.title: Luke 1:49
segments: Holy is his name. These words close the first or personal part of the hymn, Mary's praise and thanks.

entries.title: Luke 1:52
segments:
He hath put down princes from their thrones. He hath made nought of the physical force commanded by the rulers of the earth.
 

 
Hath exalted them of low degree. Hath put into the places of power those who are 'meek and lowly of heart.'  See

entries.title: Luke 1:54
segments: He hath given help to Israel, etc.  Here are manifest the Jewish and patriotic, though limited, character and application of Mary's words.  So far, apparently, she had no thought of Jehovah as God of the Gentiles.  Nevertheless the latter part of the hymn,
, taken as a whole, declares unmistakably that the kingdom of the Spirit-the rule of divine mercy, justice and truth-had forever displaced the kingdom of worldly pride and strength.

entries.title: Luke 1:56
segments: Returned unto her house. It was not until after Mary's return to Nazareth that Joseph discovered the reason for her long absence.  See

entries.title: Luke 1:59
segments: The eighth day. According to the Mosaic Law the rite of circumcision was performed upon Jewish male children on the eighth day after birth.  The rite was a symbol of purification, by which the child was prepared for the privileges of a member of the Jewish community.  He was also named at this time.

entries.title: Luke 1:63
segments: A writing tablet. Wooden and covered with wax or sand.

entries.title: Luke 1:68
segments: Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, etc.  These and the following words of

are known as the Benedictus, which takes its name from the Latin word for 'blessed.'  The Benedictus is a Christian hymn that has been used in public church services probably since the sixth century.  The prophet Zacharias, freed from the dumbness imposed upon him for his doubt, spoke in a strain of mingled blessing and prophecy.  The first part of his utterance,
, is an offering of praise and thanks to God for the fulfillment of His covenant in the birth of the Messiah; the second part,

, is in honor of his son, afterward known as John the Baptist, who was to be the Messiah's forerunner and the preacher of repentance as a preparation for his coming.  The Benedictus, like the Magnificat, is thoroughly Jewish in feeling and outlook. Zacharias had only a dim apprehension of the far-reaching significance of his words.  He had no more thought of the Gentiles than had Mary, and he was the unconscious instrument of divine purposes which embraced all mankind.

entries.title: Luke 1:69
segments: A horn of salvation. A figure of speech and often used to symbolize strength, and here applied to the Messiah.

entries.title: Luke 1:76
segments: Before the face of the Lord. An announcement of John's mission as the forerunner of Jesus.

entries.title: Luke 1:77
segments: To give knowledge of salvation, etc.  The 'knowledge' of salvation was communicated to the Jews in John's prophetic declaration that the kingdom of heaven was at hand; but it was fully realized only by those who repented, thereby obtaining the remission of their sins.

entries.title: Luke 1:78
segments: The dayspring. The dawn.

entries.title: Luke 1:79
segments: The way of peace. The true aim and end of the Messianic kingdom; the way of spiritual as well as of earthly peace.
